young.html: Luigi Pirandello was an Italian playwright who loved puzzles about what is real and what is pretend.

In his most famous play, a company of actors is rehearsing on an empty stage. Suddenly six strangers walk in: a father, a mother and four children. They say they are characters from a story whose author never finished writing it. They want the actors to play their story, so they can live it at last. The actors try, but the characters keep saying, "No, that's not how it was!" By the end, no one is sure what was real.

young.html: For parents: the characters' own story involves a painful family scandal, hinted at in the play but not shown, and it ends in tragedy for the two youngest. The lesson keeps it general.

Characters come alive. Make up a character: give them a name, a favorite food, and one problem. Then let someone else play your character in a short scene. Did they get it right? Did your character seem to "want" something you didn't plan?

full.html: Luigi Pirandello (1867–1936) was born in Sicily, studied in Rome and Bonn, and wrote novels, hundreds of short stories and some forty plays. Family misfortune, including his wife's long mental illness, shaped his interest in how differently people see the same events. Six Characters in Search of an Author was first staged in Rome in 1921, where the first-night audience was in an uproar. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1934. Edward Storer's English translation appeared in 1922.
A Manager and his actors are rehearsing a play (one of Pirandello's own) on a bare stage. Six people dressed in mourning arrive. The Father explains:

full.text: As a matter of fact … we have come here in search of an author …
full.author: Pirandello
full.work: Six Characters in Search of an Author, Act I
full.ed: Three Plays (E. P. Dutton & Co., New York)

full.html: The Manager's first reaction is impatience:

full.text: Will you oblige me by going away? We haven't time to waste with mad people.
full.author: Pirandello
full.work: Six Characters in Search of an Author, Act I
full.ed: Three Plays (E. P. Dutton & Co., New York)

full.html: But the characters' story is gripping. The Father once sent the Mother away to live with another man, and she had three more children; after years of poverty, the family's paths crossed again in a painful, shameful way. The Stepdaughter wants it all shown; the Father wants to explain himself; the Son wants no part of it. When the actors try to play the scenes, the characters protest that the actors' version is false. The Father insists that characters are more real than actors:

full.text: Because a character has really a life of his own, marked with his especial characteristics; for which reason he is always “somebody.”
full.author: Pirandello
full.work: Six Characters in Search of an Author, Act III
full.ed: Three Plays (E. P. Dutton & Co., New York)

full.html: A person changes from day to day, the Father says, but a character's moment is fixed forever. The play ends in a sudden double tragedy for the two youngest children, and the actors cannot tell whether it was real or acted. The Manager, exasperated, has lost a whole day's rehearsal.

full.html: Pirandello turns the theater inside out. The play is about the making of a play, and it asks whether anyone, on stage or off, can show the truth of another person's life.
Plays about plays were not new (Hamlet stages one), but Pirandello made the frame itself the drama. Later "metatheater," from Brecht to Beckett, owes him a great deal.
Thinking the characters are ghosts or lunatics. In the play's own terms they are exactly what they say: characters, alive in the imagination, with no finished play to live in.

items: Aristotle's Poetics, earlier on this ladder, says a drama imitates an action; Pirandello asks who decides which version of the action is true.
Cervantes, in Don Quixote Part II, lets characters read and argue about their own book, an ancestor of Pirandello's game.
Brecht and Beckett, later in this era, also break the illusion of the stage in different ways.
Pirandello's other plays, such as Right You Are (If You Think So), show a town unable to agree on the truth about one family.
Can one person ever tell another person's story truly?
Is a character in a book in any sense real?
Why do the Father and the Stepdaughter remember the same events so differently?
Is who we are fixed, or do we change from day to day?

questions: If a character from your favorite book walked into the room, what would you ask them?
Why did the characters hate the way the actors played them?
Two people in a family can remember the same day very differently. Why?
The Father says a character is always "somebody," but a person might be "nobody." What do you think he means?
Why might audiences in 1921 have been upset by this play?
care: The characters' story involves a painful family scandal, hinted at rather than shown, and ends in the deaths of the two youngest children. The lesson keeps it general.
